result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.min_weight_matching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a minimum-weight matching among the matchings with the most edges. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L57863-L57935){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.min_weight_matching(weighted=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Minimum weight matching](/assets/graphs/min-weight-matching.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Four drivers A, B, C, D with the extra driving time of each possible pair as edge weights: A–B (2), C–D (3), A–C (1), B–D (6), and A–D (4). Among the matchings that pair everyone, the cheapest is A–B and C–D, in the accent color, total 2 + 3 = 5; the other edges are faded. The card notes that taking the cheapest edge A–C (1) would force B–D (6), a total of 7." width="100%"} A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. This method first makes the matching as large as possible (as many pairs as the graph allows) and, among all such matchings, returns one with the smallest total weight. On a graph with a perfect matching, that is the cheapest way to pair up every node. It is the right tool when edges are costs (distances, prices, travel times) and everyone should be paired. Requiring a maximum number of edges matters: without it, the cheapest matching would simply be empty. Edge direction is ignored, self-loops are never chosen, and among parallel edges only the lightest can be chosen. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. Without weights every maximum matching is equally cheap. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The IDs of the matched edges, in ascending order. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If an edge weight is not finite. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} As in NetworkX, every weight $w$ is replaced by $W + 1 - w$, where $W$ is the largest weight, and a maximum-weight matching of maximum cardinality is computed with Edmonds' blossom algorithm (see `max_weight_matching()`). Since all matchings considered have the same number of edges $k$, maximizing $\sum (W + 1 - w) = k(W + 1) - \sum w$ minimizes the original total. It runs in $O(V^3)$ time. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Four delivery drivers must be paired into two-person teams, and each edge is the extra driving time if the two share a route. The cheapest pairing matches A with B and C with D: ::: {#bbb2077e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges( [("A", "B", 2.0), ("C", "D", 3.0), ("A", "C", 1.0), ("B", "D", 6.0), ("A", "D", 4.0)] ) teams = g.min_weight_matching() [(g.get_label_from_id(e.source), g.get_label_from_id(e.target), e.weight) for e in (g.get_edge(i) for i in teams)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [('A', 'B', 2.0), ('C', 'D', 3.0)] ``` ::: ::: The cheapest single edge, A-C (1), is not used: pairing A with C would force B and D together at a cost of 6, for a total of 7 instead of 5.
